questions.question: Which responsibilities belong to the AKS-managed control plane, and which belong to customer-managed node pools?
questions.answer: AKS operates the control plane components, including the API server, scheduler, controllers, and etcd, and provides their availability and maintenance. Customers choose and govern node pools, capacity, upgrades, networking, workload configuration, and application security, while Azure manages the underlying AKS infrastructure according to the service's shared-responsibility model.

learnMore.title: Azure Kubernetes Service core concepts

questions.question: How do Pods, Deployments, ReplicaSets, and StatefulSets differ?
questions.answer: A Pod is the smallest schedulable unit and contains one or more colocated containers. A ReplicaSet maintains a requested number of equivalent Pods, while a Deployment manages ReplicaSets to provide declarative rollouts and rollbacks for usually stateless workloads. A StatefulSet manages ordered Pods that need stable identities, ordered lifecycle behavior, or persistent storage.

learnMore.title: Azure Kubernetes Service cluster and workload concepts

questions.question: When should configuration live in a ConfigMap versus a Secret, and when should a Pod consume it through environment variables versus mounted files?
questions.answer: Use a ConfigMap for non-sensitive settings and a Secret for credentials or other sensitive values, remembering that a Kubernetes Secret needs appropriate encryption and access controls rather than relying on base64 encoding. Environment variables are simple but normally remain fixed for the life of a process, whereas mounted files suit file-based consumers and can reflect updates if the application reloads them. For higher-value secrets, prefer an external store such as Azure Key Vault with the Secrets Store CSI Driver.

questions.question: What basic inputs would you choose when creating an AKS cluster and its first node pool?
questions.answer: Choose the region, supported Kubernetes version, cluster mode or tier, managed identity, API access, networking model and address ranges, and required observability integrations. In AKS Standard, the initial node pool is a System pool; choose its VM size, node count, availability zones, OS, and disk configuration, then add User pools for application workloads. AKS Automatic manages its System pool for you.

learnMore.title: Deploy an AKS cluster using Azure CLI
Create and manage multiple node pools for AKS

questions.question: How do kubeconfig, kubectl, and the Kubernetes API work together when accessing an AKS cluster?
questions.answer: A kubeconfig file defines clusters, users or authentication methods, contexts, and the current context. kubectl reads that context, obtains credentials as required, and sends authenticated HTTPS requests to the Kubernetes API server; the API server then authorizes each requested operation. Protect kubeconfig files because they can contain or enable access credentials.

learnMore.title: Control access to cluster configuration files in AKS

questions.question: How do ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer Services expose a workload differently?
questions.answer: ClusterIP exposes a stable virtual IP only inside the cluster. NodePort also opens a port on every node and forwards it to the Service, while LoadBalancer asks the cloud provider to provision an external or internal Azure load balancer that forwards to the Service. All three use selectors and endpoints to route traffic to ready backend Pods.

learnMore.title: Networking concepts for applications in AKS

questions.question: What role does an Ingress controller play between an Ingress resource and a Service?
questions.answer: An Ingress resource declares host- and path-based HTTP routing, but it does not implement that routing by itself. An Ingress controller watches the resource and configures a proxy or load balancer to accept traffic, terminate TLS when configured, and forward requests to the selected Kubernetes Service and its ready endpoints.

learnMore.title: Managed NGINX ingress with the AKS application routing add-on

questions.question: At a high level, how does Azure CNI provide Pod networking in AKS?
questions.answer: Azure CNI integrates Kubernetes networking with Azure virtual networking and configures interfaces and routes so Pods can reach other Pods, Services, and external destinations. Depending on the selected mode, Pods either receive VNet-routable addresses or use private overlay addresses translated through node addresses, so IP planning and network policy choices matter.

learnMore.title: Azure CNI networking overview for AKS

questions.question: How do a PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim, and StorageClass work together?
questions.answer: A PersistentVolume represents storage available to the cluster, and a PersistentVolumeClaim is a workload's request for storage with particular size and access characteristics. A StorageClass describes how a storage backend should provision volumes; with dynamic provisioning, a matching claim causes a volume to be created and bound to that claim.

learnMore.title: Storage concepts for applications in AKS

questions.question: What is the difference between Microsoft Entra authentication and Kubernetes RBAC authorization?
questions.answer: Microsoft Entra authentication establishes who the user, group, or service principal is and supplies an identity token to the AKS API server. Kubernetes RBAC authorization then decides whether that identity may perform a verb on a resource in a namespace or cluster scope; AKS can also use Azure RBAC for Kubernetes authorization instead.

questions.question: How would you limit access to Kubernetes Secrets for a team?
questions.answer: Place Secrets in an appropriate namespace and bind the team's Microsoft Entra group to a namespace-scoped Role that grants only the required verbs on only the required Secret resources. Avoid broad list or watch permissions and cluster-wide bindings, verify access with authorization checks, and audit changes; for stronger separation, mount secrets from Azure Key Vault without granting users direct read access to Kubernetes Secret objects.

learnMore.title: Use Kubernetes RBAC with Microsoft Entra ID in AKS

questions.question: When does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) add Pods, and when does the Cluster Autoscaler add nodes?
questions.answer: The HPA changes a workload's replica count when observed metrics, such as CPU or memory utilization relative to requests, differ from its target. The Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when Pods remain unschedulable because existing nodes lack capacity, and it can remove underused nodes when their Pods can be moved safely. Accurate resource requests and sensible minimum and maximum bounds are essential for both mechanisms.

questions.question: A new Deployment has zero ready replicas; which Kubernetes objects and events would you inspect first?
questions.answer: Start with the Deployment conditions and rollout status, then inspect its ReplicaSet and Pods to learn whether creation, scheduling, startup, or readiness failed. Use describe output and namespace events before changing anything, and check current and previous container logs if containers started. Compare selectors, image references, probes, resource requests, and the new revision with the last known-good release, then pause or roll back only when the evidence supports it.

learnMore.title: AKS triage for workload deployments

questions.question: A Pod remains Pending after deployment; what basic scheduling and capacity checks would you perform?
questions.answer: Describe the Pod and read scheduler events first to identify insufficient CPU, memory, or specialized resources, unmatched affinity, untolerated taints, unbound storage, or quota limits. Compare requests with node allocatable capacity and inspect node readiness, labels, taints, node-pool autoscaler limits, and Azure quota. Correct the constraint or add suitable capacity based on that evidence rather than repeatedly recreating the Pod.

learnMore.title: Troubleshoot Pods that remain in a Pending state in AKS

questions.question: A LoadBalancer Service has an external IP but the application is unreachable; what would you check first?
questions.answer: Troubleshoot from the inside out: confirm the Pods are ready and reachable, then verify that the Service selector produces endpoints and that port and targetPort match the listening application. Next inspect Service events, load balancer health probes, network security groups, routes, firewalls, and network policies while preserving logs and observed configuration. Change one evidence-backed layer at a time and retest.

learnMore.title: Troubleshoot application connection issues in an AKS cluster
Use the Standard Load Balancer in AKS

questions.question: What would you do if a production Pod repeatedly enters CrashLoopBackOff immediately after a release?
questions.topic: safe first response to application failure
questions.answer: Stop further promotion, assess user impact, and preserve evidence by describing the Pod, reviewing events, and collecting current and previous container logs. Compare the failing revision's image, command, configuration, dependencies, and probes with the last known-good revision. If the release is the supported cause, perform a controlled rollback and monitor readiness and error signals rather than repeatedly deleting Pods or making untracked live edits.

learnMore.title: Troubleshoot a Pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff in AKS

questions.question: What would you do if kubectl suddenly returned authorization errors for an engineer who previously had access?
questions.answer: Capture the exact error and distinguish failed authentication from an authenticated but forbidden request before changing permissions. Verify the active kubeconfig context, refresh the engineer's Microsoft Entra sign-in, and inspect group membership plus namespace RoleBindings, ClusterRoleBindings, or Azure role assignments and their propagation. Restore only the least privilege that the engineer requires and review audit history for an unexpected access change.

questions.question: What would you do if traffic increased rapidly while Pods and nodes were both near capacity?
questions.answer: Confirm demand, latency, errors, resource saturation, unschedulable events, and HPA and Cluster Autoscaler status before changing limits. Verify resource requests, replica and node bounds, suitable VM capacity, and Azure quota, then raise safe scaling bounds or add appropriate capacity while watching probes and application dependencies. If capacity cannot arrive quickly enough, apply an established traffic-shaping or load-shedding plan and continue monitoring recovery.
